newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lebanon says Israel does nothing to end unrest.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon says Israel does nothing to end unrest.

text.p: Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri accused Israel on Saturday of doing nothing to help restore calm in the Palestinian territories after four days of fierce fighting in which nearly 70 people have died.
"Until now Israel has not taken a single step towards calming the situation," Hariri told reporters after an hour of talks with French President Jacqeus Chirac in Paris.

"It seems to me that (conservative Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin) Netanyahu is doing everything to destroy the peace process," Hariri said. "That worries me, and we are concerned because we have seen on television how they are murdering civilians".
During their talks, Hariri and Chirac made a joint appeal for a de-escalation and a return to reason in the Middle East, a Chirac aide told reporters.
"Both men spoke of their deep concern about the current situation and the need to begin working on a process to reduce tensions," the aide said without offering specifics.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette later echoed Hariri's remarks, saying Israel had simply not responded to his requests that Israel withdraw its soldiers from the Palestinian territories and permanently close down a tunnel it had opened up near a Moslem shrine in Jerusalem.

"For the time being I have not had any response. But that should not prevent us from developing additional initiatives," he said in an interview in the weekly Le Journal du Dimanche, to appear on Sunday.
De Charette added that he was prepared to return to the Middle East "at any moment" if it could contribute to peace.
Chirac had on Friday joined Prime Minister John Major and Chancellor Helmut Kohl in urging Netanyahu and Arafat to quickly meet to help restore calm in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
The three west European powers called for an immediate resumption of high-level peace talks and the full implementation of accords already reached between Israel and the PLO.
"This approach appears to us to be the only way to restore calm durably in the territories and to ensure Israel's security," they said.

Palestinian police were trying to keep a lid on protests in the West Bank and Gaza on Saturday as the United States worked frantically to arrange a meeting between Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.

The violence was ignited by Israel's decision to open a tunnel near Moslem shrines in Jerusalem. Palestinians called the tunnel's opening an assault on Islamic holy shrines and an Israeli attempt to "Judaise" Arab East Jerusalem, occupied by Israel in 1967 and later annexed.
Netanyahu's reluctance to implement the Oslo self-rule agreement, which includes a partial Israeli troop withdrawal in Hebron, fuelled Palestinian suspicion and frustration.
Chirac has been pressing hard in recent months to give France a higher profile in Middle East diplomacy.
He plans a second visit to the turbulent region next month, though a precise date for the trip has not yet been fixed.
Presidential aides said Chirac would go to Syria, Israel, Jordan and the Palestinian territories as well as Lebanon.
